Democrats in Congress say when they take control in January,
ending the U.S. participation in the war against Iran will be a top priority.
Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia said President Trump and Republicans in Congress
are forcing the Democratic majority in the House and Senate to take action.
Two Republican majority houses declared a war was illegal and ordered the president to stop it.
He is refusing to follow that resolution, and that leaves us basically only one choice.
If you won't follow the Constitution, the statute, or the concurrent resolution,
our only choice is to use the appropriations process to forbid funding for war operations
unless the president gets the legally required authorization by Congress.
Kaine said several Republicans have indicated they will support this move.
In the most recent report, the Pentagon estimates the war has cost more than $37 billion,
much of it in the cost to replace missiles and other munitions.
Two U.S. Senate races are still too close to call in both Alaska and Mississippi,
where the Democrat Scott Colum leads the Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by fewer than 2,000 votes.
From Mississippi Public Radio, Elise Katron-Greg reports.
Both candidates say they have lawyers monitoring the ballot count
and ready for legal challenges that will likely follow this race.
Here's Mississippi GOP chair Mike Hurst.
Every outstanding ballot, every county, every deadline, every legal option will get our full attention.
We will not sleep until we know that our elections are secure.
Lee Parrott, a Colum supporter, says she's cautiously optimistic about Colum winning
because of changes to Mississippi's voter roll review system.
I think a lot of names were purged, and the system that they used to purge was questionable.
Results likely won't be ready until at least Tuesday, the deadline for mail-in ballots.
For NPR News, I'm Elise Katron-Greg in Jackson.
Google, Meta, and TikTok are challenging a new California law.
Here's NPR's Katie McQuay.
California's new law prohibits social media platforms from offering features
considered exploitative to users younger than 18.
That includes using algorithms to keep kids scrolling and auto-playing video.
The law also requires social media companies to delete children's accounts with those features.
Yet the companies argue that the law is unconstitutional and violates the First Amendment.
The lawsuits come amid growing scrutiny of tech companies' impact on children.
Meta, Google, TikTok, and Snap are facing thousands of lawsuits from families,
school districts, and state governments who allege their platforms contribute to a youth mental health crisis.
Katie McQuay, NPR News, New York.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Voters are going to the polls in New Zealand to cast their ballots in the country's general election.
High inflation and housing affordability are some of the key issues.
Adam Hancock reports.
Economic issues are set to be front of mind for voters.
New Zealand is facing a cost-of-living crisis with inflation at 3.7%
and unemployment at its highest level since 2015.
There are also concerns about the availability and affordability of housing,
although property prices are now 17% below their peak in early 2022.
Polls will close at 7pm local time with preliminary results expected a few hours later.
Left-leaning parties, including Labour, are looking to make the incumbent coalition
led by the centre-right national party the first one-term government in nearly 50 years.
Official results, including overseas ballots, will be declared on November the 27th.
For NPR News, I'm Adam Hancock in Sydney.
A Venezuelan man who the Department of Homeland Security says was in the country illegally
is in custody after he was arrested Thursday night near the White House.
The Secret Service said he had multiple weapons and ammunition in a stolen car
when he was taken into custody and police believed he was acting suspicious.
Officials also said the man threatened to kill President Trump
and he heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington to shoot the president.
In a statement, Homeland Security said the man entered the United States in March of 2024 illegally
and was arrested by the Border Patrol and later arrested, released.
